text: Subagents share the container (files, HTTPS_PROXY, checkouts, branch, HEAD); only context windows are separate.
Sharing explains the shared search budget and concurrency cap.
Agents can write directly into the repo for the main loop to commit.
Agent tool `isolation: "worktree"` and `isolation: "remote"` are the exceptions to sharing.
Agent concurrency caps at 20; larger dispatches partially fail with `Concurrent subagent limit reached`.
Raise the cap with `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`.
Cap's real cost is a silent drop: a rostered item never dispatched successfully never reports.
Reconcile the roster against what launched, not what was dispatched; `ListAgents` settles it in one call.
Workflow cap is min(16, CPUs minus 2) per run (measured 2026-09-06).
This container reports 4 CPUs (`nproc`): Workflow would run two agents at a time.
Read `nproc` before choosing a fan-out venue; here the Agent tool (20) beats Workflow tenfold.
Measurements below come from one run of 124 agents, 17 minutes at the cap.
Agent tool has no effort parameter (only Workflow's `agent()` does); a low-effort instruction must go in the prompt.
Output on disk is not agent done: the agent holds its slot until it returns.
A ledger kept from file arrivals overcounts free slots by one or two.
A refused launch is cheap: count slots with `ListAgents` and relaunch.
Prompt-named validator the agent runs on its own output made 124 of 124 outputs parse and conform.
The validator is the Agent-tool equivalent of Workflow's `schema` option, and it is committed.
Cost is in the transcripts: sum each line's `message.usage` block for the agent's spend, not the notification.
Run totals: 91.3M tokens, 74.4M cache reads of the shared prompt, 300k output.
Readers averaged 105k tokens and about two minutes; skeptics 97k and about 90 seconds.
